editorial.headline: Hazardous Waste Collection With a Bali Scope Test
editorial.standfirst: This activity is nationally open to foreign ownership, but Bali registration turns on the exact declared scope and OSS risk treatment.
editorial.body:
This activity is the organised collection of non-radioactive hazardous waste and specific hazardous waste. The record describes materials that may explode, oxidise, burn, poison, irritate, corrode, cause cancer, transmit infection, or otherwise endanger human health and the environment. Its practical field is not ordinary rubbish collection; it is the front end of a controlled waste chain, where the collection process may include identifying, handling, packaging, and labelling hazardous waste so it can be transported.

The examples in the scope make the activity concrete. It includes used oil from ships or workshops, bio-hazardous waste, used batteries and accumulators, hazardous waste from animals, and expired medicines. It also includes the operation of transfer facilities for non-radioactive hazardous waste. The record further names the collection of waste containing B3 and/or B3 waste from households at facilities for managing specific waste, as well as B3 waste collection. In plain English, this is the classification for businesses whose work begins where hazardous materials are gathered, secured, and prepared for movement rather than left unmanaged at the source.

Nationally, the foreign-investment picture is straightforward. The activity is marked open, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%, sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. The scale access is also broad: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar are all listed as open. That matters because the record does not reserve the activity to a single size of operator. A founder reading this nationally would see a hazardous-waste collection activity that can be registered across the full stated scale range, including by a foreign-owned company up to the stated ceiling.

Bali needs a more careful reading. The Bali status is Blocked (scope-dependent), while the blocked flag is false. That means the record does not treat this as categorically closed in Bali, but it also does not give a simple island-wide green light. The reason says OSS risk at Besar scale is low for some scopes and higher for others, and that PMA registration in Bali is available only by declaring the higher-risk scope, with live OSS verification required for the exact activity. The underlying Bali rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province on a permanent basis. So the honest position is this: nationally, the activity is open up to 100% foreign ownership; in Bali, a PMA setup depends on the precise declared scope and its OSS risk treatment, not merely on the broad title of hazardous-waste collection.
